items.title: What a second Cancel changes
items.body:
`Cancel` checks the start rule and then wraps all its work in `if (!_isCanceled)`. The first call sets the flag, the date and member A, and adds `MeetingCanceledDomainEvent`. The second call, still before the start, passes the start rule, finds the flag set and does nothing: no new event, and the stored member stays A. After the start the same call would throw from the start rule instead.

- Before the start, a repeat call does not throw.
- B is never written, because the block that assigns the member is skipped.
- No second event is added; the event is inside the same block.

excerpts.quote: It leaves the original cancel date and member unchanged and adds no second cancellation event.

items.title: Why the exact start instant still allows changes
items.body:
`MeetingCannotBeChangedAfterStartRule` asks `MeetingTerm.IsAfterStart()`, which returns `SystemClock.Now > this.StartDate`. At exact equality the comparison is false, so the rule is not broken. One tick later it is true. The course recommends testing one tick before, exactly at and one tick after the start.

- Started means strictly after `StartDate` in this code.
- There is no grace window in the rule.
- `SystemClock` returns the time it is given; no rounding is involved.

excerpts.quote: At exactly start, it is still not broken.

items.title: Start here: the Meetings aggregate and its rule classes
items.body:
This repository wraps Kamil Grzybek's `modular-monolith-with-ddd`, a .NET sample of a modular monolith built with domain-driven design, plus a course in `astraupskill/`. The quest stays inside one module: Meetings.

Read in this order:

1. `astraupskill/01-CODEBASE-MAP.md` and `02-CONCEPTS.md`: one small invariant (a meeting term must have positive duration) traced from command to value object.
2. `astraupskill/advanced/extended-course/03` (two kinds of term), then `07` to `10` (capacity, roles, waitlists, cancellation and time).

Keep three places open while you read: `Domain/Meetings/Meeting.cs` (the aggregate root), `MeetingAttendee.cs` (one child record per attendance) and the `Rules/` folder. Each business rule is a tiny class with an `IsBroken()` expression, and the aggregate calls `CheckRule` with it; a broken rule throws `BusinessRuleValidationException`. Most questions in this quest are answered by reading one `IsBroken()` line and the order of the `CheckRule` calls around it. The course chapters are careful to separate what the code does today from proposed changes; the quiz is about today's code.

excerpts.quote: The established CheckRule mechanism throws BusinessRuleValidationException with the broken rule attached, keeping the failure consistent with other domain invariants.

readMore.why: The course overview and reading route.

items.title: Why a guest limit of 0 allows four guests
items.body:
The guest rule is `_guestsLimit > 0 && _guestsLimit < _guestsNumber`. With a limit of 0 the first half is false, so the rule can never break: 0 switches the check off rather than banning guests. The total rule needs `_attendeesLimit.HasValue`, and a null limit fails that test, so it cannot break either. Nothing stops the request.

- 0 is not a prohibition in this expression; the course calls this out as a source observation.
- Null means no total ceiling, not zero places.
- `MeetingLimits.Create(null, 0)` is valid: neither limit is negative and the greater-than rule needs a value.

excerpts.quote: Consequently, zero currently disables this particular upper-bound check; it does not mean that zero guests are permitted.

items.title: Why a removed attendee cannot rejoin
items.body:
`MemberCannotBeAnAttendeeOfMeetingMoreThanOnceRule` is broken when any record matches `IsActiveAttendee(memberId)`. That predicate checks only the member id and `!_decisionChanged`. `Remove` sets `_isRemoved` and a removal date, but not `_decisionChanged`, so the removed record still matches and the new request is rejected as a duplicate. Capacity uses `IsActive`, which does look at `_isRemoved`, so the same record no longer takes a place.

- The record still matches the duplicate lookup, so it does count there.
- No code path reactivates an old record.
- Removal from a meeting does not touch group membership.

items.title: Why Ben is promoted although no seat was freed
items.body:
`AddNotAttendee` adds the not-attendee record, looks up an attendee for the member and calls `attendee?.ChangeDecision()`. For Cara the lookup returns null, so nothing changes. The method then takes the first active waitlist member by sign-up date and, if there is one, creates an attendee for them. That step has no condition on the lookup result, does not run the `AddAttendee` rules and passes 0 guests.

- Promotion is not tied to a freed place in this code.
- No capacity rule runs on this path.
- The promoted attendee always gets 0 guests.

excerpts.quote: Promotion is not visibly conditional on finding an attendee to free a place.

items.title: Why the zero-guest member does not fit
items.body:
Occupied places come from `GetAllActiveAttendeesWithGuestsNumber`: every active attendee contributes `1 + guests`. The creator host is an attendee, so the count starts at 1; the member with three guests adds 4, making 5. The total rule is broken when `limit < occupied + 1 + requested guests`, here 5 < 5 + 1 + 0, so the request is rejected by `MeetingAttendeesNumberIsAboveLimitRule`.

- Counting records (2) instead of places forgets the guests.
- The host is not exempt; it is an active attendee with a place.
- The guest rule passes, since 0 guests is under any guest limit.

items.title: Concept: time, history and the order of mutation
items.body:
Three more ideas run through chapters 03, 08, 09 and 10.

**Time is an input.** The domain reads `SystemClock.Now`, which tests can set. Any boundary question becomes a question about one comparison operator. Read `MeetingTerm.IsAfterStart`, `MeetingTermMustEndAfterStartRule` and `Term.IsInTerm` and write each operator down.

**History is kept, not deleted.** Signing off a waitlist, changing a decision or removing an attendee sets flags and dates on an existing record; the collection keeps it. Follow one member through two waitlist records and note which predicate decides which record counts.

**Order of checks and changes.** For `SetHostRole` and `SetAttendeeRole`, list every statement in order, including the calls into the child, and mark which ones check a rule and which ones change state.

What else to look for: in `AddNotAttendee`, every condition that guards the waitlist promotion and every argument passed to `MeetingAttendee.CreateNew`; in `Cancel`, what the `_isCanceled` flag guards; and which other methods in `Meeting.cs` read that flag at all.

excerpts.quote: Lifecycle commands are often described as idempotent or forbidden after start. Those phrases conceal important qualifications.

items.title: Why the last host is changed before the rule throws
items.body:
`SetAttendeeRole` passes its three early checks, then calls `attendee.SetAsAttendee()`. Inside the child, the already-attendee rule passes (the creator is a host), the role becomes Attendee and `MemberSetAsAttendeeDomainEvent` is appended. Only after that does `Meeting` count active hosts, find 0, and throw `MeetingMustHaveAtLeastOneHostRule`. Nothing restores the role or removes the event, so the in-memory aggregate is changed even though the call failed.

- The host count is checked after the mutation, not before.
- The rule does throw, so the call does not succeed.
- Acting on yourself is allowed; the creator is both actor and target here.

items.title: Which fee a promoted member pays
items.body:
The promotion builds `MeetingAttendee.CreateNew(..., 0, this._eventFee)`, passing the meeting's event fee as it is at promotion time. The child constructor computes `(1 + guestsNumber) * eventFee`, and with 0 guests that is the fee itself: 15. `MeetingWaitlistMember` stores no fee, so nothing from sign-up time could be used.

- There is no fee field on the waitlist record to snapshot 10.
- `MoneyValue.Undefined` is used for hosts created with the meeting, not for promotions.
- 0 guests means one place, so the fee is not doubled.

excerpts.quote: The promotion code supplies the current meeting fee when constructing the attendee, not a fee snapshot stored on the waitlist member.

items.title: Why Ben goes before Ada
items.body:
Promotion selects `_waitlistMembers.Where(x => x.IsActive()).OrderBy(x => x.SignUpDate).FirstOrDefault()`. Ada's 09:00 record was signed off, so it is no longer active and is filtered out. The active records are Ben (09:05) and Ada's second record (09:15). Ordered by sign-up date, Ben is first.

- Ada's earliest record is history, not a place in the queue.
- Signing up again creates a new record; the old one is never reactivated.
- Promotion is triggered by `AddNotAttendee`, not by sign-offs.

items.title: Why the start-time rule wins
items.body:
`CheckRule` throws as soon as one rule is broken, so the order of the calls decides which rule a caller sees. `AddAttendee` checks the start time first, then RSVP term, group membership, duplicates, the guest limit and total capacity. After the start, the first rule already breaks and none of the others runs. The chapter's advice follows: to test capacity, make every earlier rule pass first.

- The guest rule is fifth in line and never evaluated here.
- Group membership is third; also never reached.
- Total capacity runs last, not first.

excerpts.quote: The capacity numbers may be invalid, but the observed first rule is the start-time rule.

items.title: Why a cancelled meeting still accepts attendees
items.body:
Only `Cancel` reads `_isCanceled`. `AddAttendee` runs its own six rules (start time, RSVP term, group membership, duplicates, guest limit, total capacity) and none of them looks at the cancellation flag. For an eligible member inside the RSVP term before the start, every rule passes and the attendee is appended. The course warns not to draw cancellation as a terminal state unless the code enforces it.

- Nothing in the domain treats cancellation as terminal.
- The start rule depends on the clock, not on cancellation.
- New attendees are never created as removed.

excerpts.quote: The selected AddAttendee, role, waitlist, and removal methods visibly check their own guards; they do not automatically inherit the Cancel method's flag branch.

items.title: Why equal limits are rejected
items.body:
`MeetingLimits.Create` checks three rules, and the last is `MeetingAttendeesLimitMustBeGreaterThanGuestsLimitRule`. It is broken when an attendee limit exists and is `<=` the guest limit. 5 <= 5 is true, so the factory throws a `BusinessRuleValidationException`.

- Equal limits are exactly the case the `<=` rejects.
- The factory never adjusts a value; it either accepts or throws.
- This is configuration validation; it runs when the limits are created, not when attendees join.
